title: Varanasi & Sarnath
selection: Uttar Pradesh had the most domestic tourist visits of any state in 2024 (646.81 million) and 2.27 million foreign visits (India Tourism Data Compendium 2025). places.name: Varanasi
places.summary: Kashi, the city of light: dawn on the Ganga, the evening aarti at Dashashwamedh, temples, silk and lanes — with Sarnath next door.
places.seoTitle: Varanasi Travel Guide: Ghats, Ganga Aarti & Sarnath
places.seoDescription: Plan your Varanasi trip: the ghats and Ganga Aarti, a dawn boat ride, Kashi Vishwanath, Sarnath, when to go, getting there, food, etiquette and a 3-day itinerary.

images.alt: Rowing boats on the Ganga beside a ghat in Varanasi in the early morning
images.caption: Morning on the ghats, Varanasi

overview.text:
Varanasi — also known as Kashi and Banaras — is one of the world's oldest living cities and one of Hinduism's seven sacred cities. Its riverfront is lined with at least 84 ghats, stone steps down to the Ganga where pilgrims bathe and pray at dawn and where, at a few ghats such as Manikarnika, the dead are cremated. Life and death sit side by side here, openly, and that is what makes the city so moving.

The rhythm of a visit follows the river: a boat ride at sunrise, the old city's lanes and temples by day, and the Ganga Aarti at Dashashwamedh Ghat every evening. Varanasi is also a UNESCO City of Music and the home of the Banarasi silk sari. Just 8 km away is Sarnath, where the Buddha gave his first sermon — a World Heritage Site since 2026.

October to March is the most pleasant time to visit. Allow at least two full days, three with Sarnath.

items.body: A dawn boat ride past the ghats as the city bathes and prays.
The Ganga Aarti at Dashashwamedh Ghat, every evening.
Subah-e-Banaras at Assi Ghat: chants, music and yoga at sunrise.
Kashi Vishwanath Temple and the lanes of the old city.
Sarnath, where the Buddha gave his first sermon.

best_time.text:
The Ministry of Tourism recommends October to March, when the weather suits walking the ghats and taking boat rides; winter mornings often bring fog over the river. The dry summer, from April to June, is very hot, and the monsoon lasts from July to October.

Festivals add another reason to time a trip: Dev Deepawali, fifteen days after Diwali, when thousands of lamps light the ghats, is the most spectacular — and the busiest, so book rooms early.

how_to_reach.text:
By air: Lal Bahadur Shastri International Airport (VNS) is about 25 km from the city centre, with domestic and some international flights.

By train: Varanasi is a major rail hub. Check which station your train uses — Varanasi Junction (BSB), Banaras (BSBS), Pt. Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Junction (DDU, some way out of town) or Kashi (KEI).

By road: buses and taxis connect Varanasi with Prayagraj, Ayodhya, Lucknow, Bodh Gaya and Gorakhpur.

local_transport.text: The old city and the ghats are best explored on foot — many lanes are too narrow for cars. Walking along the riverfront between ghats is easy for much of the year, and boats ply the river from the main ghats. Use auto-rickshaws or taxis for the airport, the stations, Ramnagar Fort and Sarnath, and agree the fare first.

where_to_stay.text: Guesthouses and small hotels along and just behind the ghats put the river at your door — ideal for dawn boat rides and the evening aarti, though access is on foot through narrow lanes. The Assi Ghat area is a little calmer and has many cafes. Larger hotels with easier road access are further from the river. The Kashi Vishwanath temple trust also runs guest houses near the temple and the ghats.

items.body: Breakfast on kachori sabzi, then try tamatar chaat and choora matar.
Malaiyyo, a frothy milk sweet, in winter.
Banarasi lassi and chai.
Banarasi paan, a GI-recognised symbol of the city.
Walk the old-city lanes — Vishwanath Gali, Kachauri Gali and Thatheri Bazaar.
Shop for a Banarasi silk sari (look for the GI tag).
Visit the Bharat Mata Temple's marble relief map of India and the Sankat Mochan Temple.
Cross the river to Ramnagar Fort and its royal museum.
At the cremation ghats, keep a respectful distance and never photograph cremations or mourners.
Dress modestly and remove your shoes at temples.
Ask before photographing pilgrims bathing or sadhus, and expect some to ask for a tip.
Many places near the river are vegetarian and alcohol-free.

items.title: Visas
items.body: Apply for an e-Tourist visa at least 4 days before arrival; your passport needs at least six months' validity.

items.title: Payments
items.body: Visitors can pay by QR code with NPCI's UPI One World wallet after a passport-and-visa KYC check. Carry cash for boats, rickshaws and small shops.

items.title: Boats
items.body: Agree the price and duration before getting into a boat.

items.title: Emergency
items.body: Dial 112 for police, fire or ambulance.

items.title: The river
items.body: Currents can be strong — avoid swimming, and keep to the boat when on the water.

items.title: Crowds
items.body: The evening aarti and festivals draw very large crowds; keep valuables secure and agree a meeting point.

items.title: Heat
items.body: From April to June, go out early and late and drink plenty of water.

items.title: When is the Ganga Aarti?
items.body: Every evening at Dashashwamedh Ghat; it lasts about 45 minutes. Watch from the steps or from a boat.

items.title: How far is Sarnath from Varanasi?
items.body: About 8 km north-east — an easy half-day trip.

items.title: Can I visit the cremation ghats?
items.body: Yes, respectfully and from a distance. Photography of cremations is not appropriate.

items.title: How many days do I need?
items.body: Two full days for the ghats and old city; add a third for Sarnath.
Get up for sunrise at least once — the river is at its most beautiful.
Book the Kashi Vishwanath Sugam Darshan in advance if you want to skip the queue.
For Dev Deepawali, book rooms and boats well ahead.

places.summary: Varanasi's busiest ghat and the stage for the Ganga Aarti every evening.

overview.text:
Dashashwamedh is the liveliest of Varanasi's ghats and the stage for the city's best-known ritual: the Ganga Aarti, held every evening. As dusk falls, priests of the Gangotri Seva Samiti stand on raised platforms facing the river and offer fire to the Ganga, swinging tiered brass lamps in unison to the sound of bells, conch shells and chanted mantras. The ceremony lasts about forty-five minutes.

You can watch from the ghat steps, which fill up well before the start, or from a boat moored on the river. Legend says the god Brahma performed ten Ashwamedh sacrifices here, which gives the ghat its name. The ghat is open at all hours, and is especially magical during Dev Deepawali, when thousands of lamps line the river.

items.title: Ganga Aarti
items.body: Every evening at dusk; about 45 minutes.

items.title: Where to watch
items.body: From the steps (arrive early) or from a boat on the river.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: Open at all hours.
Arrive 45–60 minutes early for a spot on the steps.

overview.text:
Assi Ghat lies at the southern end of Varanasi's riverfront, where the small Assi river meets the Ganga. Mornings here begin with Subah-e-Banaras, a session of Vedic chants, prayers and music followed by yoga and meditation as the sun comes up over the river.

Assi is also a good place to start a boat ride, watch the smaller evening aarti, or linger in the many cafes and restaurants nearby — it is calmer than the ghats around Dashashwamedh. Pilgrims also visit Lolarka Kund, an ancient sacred tank fifteen metres below ground, reached by steep steps.

items.title: Subah-e-Banaras
items.body: Every morning at sunrise.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: Open at all hours.
Come before sunrise for Subah-e-Banaras, then take a boat north along the ghats.
Visit during the Magh Mela (January–February) or Dev Deepawali to see Assi at its liveliest — and busiest.
The cafes around the ghat are a good place to rest between sights.

places.seoDescription: Manikarnika Ghat in Varanasi is one of Hinduism's holiest cremation grounds. What it is, where it is and how to visit respectfully.

overview.text: Manikarnika, between Dashashwamedh and Scindia ghats, is one of the holiest sites for cremation in Hindu tradition. Its southern part is reserved for cremations, which continue day and night; the northern part is used for bathing rituals. Visitors may watch from a respectful distance or from a boat, but never photograph cremations or the families of the dead.

overview.text: The Kashi Vishwanath Temple, dedicated to Shiva and known as the Golden Temple, is the spiritual heart of Varanasi; the present temple was built in 1780 by Maharani Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore. Since December 2021 the Kashi Vishwanath Corridor has linked it directly with the ghats. Queues can be long: the temple trust's 'Sugam Darshan' is a booked, queue-less visit with an escort and a free locker. The trust's helpline is +91 6393 131 608.

overview.text:
Ramnagar Fort stands on the east bank of the Ganga, opposite Tulsi Ghat. It was built in red sandstone in the 18th century by Maharaja Balwant Singh, ruler of Kashi, and is the ancestral home of the Maharajas of Banaras. You can reach it by a 30-minute boat ride from the ghats or by road.

The museum inside displays the royal family's treasures: vintage cars, palanquins, costumes, an armoury and a rare 19th-century astronomical clock. Ramnagar is also famous for its month-long Ramlila, a performance of the Ramayana staged across the town.

items.body: 10 am – 5 pm.

items.title: Getting there
items.body: About 30 minutes by boat from the ghats, or by road.
Tour the museum's vintage cars, palanquins, royal costumes and armoury.
Find the 19th-century astronomical clock.

overview.text:
According to Buddhist texts, it was at Sarnath, after his enlightenment, that the Buddha met his first disciples and gave his first sermon — the moment regarded as the beginning of Buddhism's spread. Over the centuries stupas, temples and monasteries grew up here, and Sarnath became one of the four key destinations of Buddhist pilgrimage. In July 2026 it was inscribed as India's 45th UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The site lies about 8 km north-east of Varanasi. Its centrepiece is the Deer Park, with the 42 m Dhamekh Stupa and the Dharmarajika Stupa among the excavated monasteries; nearby, the Chaukhandi Stupa marks where the Buddha met his first five disciples. Don't miss the Sarnath Museum, built around the Lion Capital of Ashoka, and the Mulagandha Kuti Vihara temple. In 2024–25 the excavated remains drew 744,213 Indian and 59,086 foreign visitors.

items.title: Visiting hours
items.body: The Ministry of Tourism lists 8 am – 6 pm. Check the museum's hours and weekly closing day separately before you go.

items.title: Getting there
items.body: About 8 km from Varanasi by auto-rickshaw or taxi.

items.title: Tickets
items.body: Check current fees on the Archaeological Survey of India's official site.
Start at the Chaukhandi Stupa, then walk the Deer Park and finish at the museum.
Allow half a day; mornings are quieter and cooler.
Dress modestly and walk clockwise around the stupas, as pilgrims do.

itineraries.summary: Evening aarti on arrival, a sunrise boat ride and the old city's temples and lanes, then a morning at Sarnath where the Buddha first taught.
itineraries.seoTitle: 3 Days in Varanasi Itinerary: Ghats, Aarti & Sarnath
itineraries.seoDescription: A realistic three-day Varanasi itinerary: the Ganga Aarti, a dawn boat ride, Subah-e-Banaras, Kashi Vishwanath, Ramnagar Fort and a half day at Sarnath.

plan.overview: Varanasi runs to the river's timetable: up before dawn, a slow middle of the day, and the aarti at dusk. This plan keeps mornings and evenings for the ghats and uses the hot middle hours for the old city, museums and rest. Most of it is on foot.

stops.name: Check in near the ghats and rest
Walk the riverfront north from Assi Ghat
Ganga Aarti at Dashashwamedh Ghat
stops.note: Arrive early for a spot, or watch from a boat.

days.title: Sunrise on the river and the old city

stops.name: Kashi Vishwanath Temple and the old-city lanes
stops.note: Book Sugam Darshan to skip the queue. Phones and bags may need to go in a locker.

stops.name: Ramnagar Fort
stops.note: Open until 5 pm; go by road or a 30-minute boat ride.

days.meals: Kachori sabzi for breakfast; lassi in the lanes.

days.title: Sarnath

stops.name: Sarnath: Chaukhandi Stupa, the Deer Park and the Dhamekh Stupa
stops.note: About 8 km from Varanasi. Visit the museum too.

stops.name: Silk shopping or onward travel
stops.note: Look for the GI tag on Banarasi silk.

days.travel: Auto-rickshaw or taxi to Sarnath, about 8 km each way.
days.overnight: Varanasi, or onward by train or flight

budget.assumptions: Monument fees (Sarnath, Ramnagar Fort) couldn't be confirmed from an official page during research, so check them before you go. The ghats and the aarti are free. Accommodation, boats, transport and meals are not estimated.

lines.label: Sarnath site, museum and Ramnagar Fort

booking.detail: Book through the temple trust's official website.
Book well ahead for Dev Deepawali.
Check which Varanasi station your train uses before booking on IRCTC.

alternatives: Two days only? Do Sarnath on the morning of Day 2 and the old city in the afternoon.
Swap Ramnagar Fort for the Bharat Mata Temple or the Sankat Mochan Temple.
Add a day trip to Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha attained enlightenment (several hours by road).
tips: Never photograph cremations at Manikarnika or Harishchandra ghats.
Carry small change for boats and rickshaws.
